A1-A2.headline: Knights and Tournaments in the Middle Ages

pages.text: In the Middle Ages, knights practiced for war by joining tournaments. These were big and popular shows where knights could fight in groups and show their strength. People held them for weddings, birthdays, or just for fun.
pages.caption: An early 14th century depiction of mounted combat in a tournament from the German Codex Manesse

evidence.articleCaption: An early 14th century depiction of mounted combat in a tournament from the German Codex Manesse

pages.text: The main part of a tournament was the melee. This was a large fight where two teams of knights rode at each other in an open field. They wore full armor and used swords, maces, and shields.
pages.caption: Two teams stand ready just before the match begins; each side has 24 knights, each with a banner-bearer. There is a central spectators' box for the four judges, and one on each side for the ladies; inscribed over the boxes is plus est en vous which is the motto of the Gruuthuse family of Bruges.

pages.text: Before the main fight, knights often did single combats called jousts. Two knights rode horses toward each other with long lances. Jousts were also held on the evening before the big day.

pages.text: Hundreds of knights traveled from many places to join these famous events. They came from England, Germany, France, and other regions. Large crowds watched the battles from special wooden stands near the field.
pages.caption: The joust outlasted the tournament proper and was widely practiced well into the 16th century (sketch by Jörg Breu the Elder, 1510).

pages.text: After the fighting ended, the host gave out big meals and prizes to the best knights. Most tournaments lasted until everyone was very tired or until the sun went down.

During the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, tournaments served as popular chivalrous competitions. Communities organized these mock fights for coronations, weddings, or simply as entertainment, though some critics viewed them as frivolous and a threat to public order.

pages.text: Major tournaments in northern France and England drew hundreds of foreign knights from across Europe. Spectators watched from stands while participants stayed in designated lodgings before gathering on the field for the opening review and charge.

Battles usually continued across several square miles until both sides grew completely exhausted or fading light ended the day. Afterward, patrons hosted lavish banquets to award prizes to the best fighters on each side.

pages.text: Timbuktu is an ancient city in Mali. It is situated twenty kilometres north of the Niger River. It serves as the capital of the Tombouctou Region. The population of the city was around eighty-four thousand people according to the 2023 census.

pages.text: The city started as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century. Later, it became part of the Mali Empire early in the 14th century.

pages.text: During its golden age, Timbuktu became an important centre of learning and trade in Africa. Its scholars studied Islamic studies, history, law, science, and medicine. Tales of the city created a mysterious reputation in Europe, and different groups governed until France took control in 1893.

C1-C2.headline: The Legacy and Evolution of Timbuktu

pages.text: Repatriation is the return of cultural items to their home countries or former owners. These objects are often ancient or looted art. They can be sculptures, paintings, monuments, or human remains taken during wars or imperial conquests. People have taken such valuable items from defeated groups since ancient times across the world.

pages.text: Napoleon's army took many artworks from countries like Italy and Spain. After Napoleon lost, the Duke of Wellington returned some of these items to Italy. This was a new idea because victors usually kept their spoils. However, about half of the plundered art remained in France because museum directors had hidden many important works away.

pages.text: In later years, laws and rules tried to protect cultural property during wars. Abraham Lincoln asked for a legal code to protect cultural sites from attacks. Later, international meetings like the Hague Convention created rules against pillaging. The 1970 UNESCO Convention also helped member states seize stolen objects with proper documentation in museums.

While challenges remain, people continue to discuss the fair treatment of cultural property taken during past conflicts, colonial rules, and wars around the globe.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Debates of Cultural Property Repatriation

pages.text: Repatriation refers to returning cultural property, such as ancient or looted art, to its country of origin or former owners. Disputed items include physical artifacts taken during imperialism, colonialism, or war. Contested objects vary widely from sculptures and paintings to human remains and tools. The looting of cultural heritage by victorious forces has been a common practice since ancient times.
pages.caption: The Horses of Saint Mark; looted by the Republic of Venice in the Sack of Constantinople in 1204, then by the Revolution Army of Italy led by Bonaparte from Venice in 1797, but repatriated to Italy in 1815.

pages.text: During the Napoleonic Wars, French forces systematically confiscated artworks across Europe on an unprecedented scale. After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo, the Duke of Wellington decided to return plundered art to Italy and other nations, departing from the traditional view that victors keep their spoils. Despite public outcry in France and efforts to hide works, an estimated fifty-five percent of the seized art was repatriated.

pages.text: Various international conventions attempted to curb wartime plundering. In 1863, President Abraham Lincoln commissioned the Lieber Code, which legally recognized cultural property as a protected category during war and influenced later Hague Conventions. Subsequent international agreements, such as the 1970 UNESCO Convention, aided member states in recovering illicitly exported and stolen objects through proper institutional documentation.

pages.text: In the early twenty-first century, acquisitions by Western collections faced heightened scrutiny regarding their colonial contexts. Following a 2018 French report on African cultural heritage, international debates sparked changes in museum roles and prompted restitutions based on moral rather than strictly legal grounds. Meanwhile, nations like the United Kingdom rely on museum guidelines rather than formal national legislation to manage repatriation claims.

pages.text: Legislative frameworks continue to evolve across different countries. For instance, a French law adopted in 2026 simplified the restitution process for items acquired during the colonial era through specific decrees and expert commissions. pages.text: The history of human flight started a long time ago. People made kites in China many years before the common era. These kites used light bamboo and silk. Later, inventors tried to jump from towers with fake wings, but this was very dangerous.

pages.text: In the eighteenth century, the Montgolfier brothers made the first hot-air balloon. People also invented hydrogen balloons around the same time. These balloons let humans fly into the sky and helped scientists learn more about the air and altitude.

pages.text: Cholera is a serious infection in the small intestine. It comes from some types of bacteria found in water and food. People can get very sick with watery diarrhea. This can lead to fast and dangerous loss of water in the body.
pages.caption: Typical cholera diarrhea that looks like "rice water"

pages.text: The illness spreads mostly through unsafe water and food with bacteria. Bad sanitation and poverty are big risk factors. Humans are the only known host for these bacteria. Undercooked shellfish can also be a common source of the disease.

pages.text: Doctors treat cholera mainly with special oral rehydration salts. Patients must replace lost fluids and body salts quickly. In very bad cases, people might need fluids through a vein and helpful medicines called antibiotics to get better.

pages.text: Cholera is an acute diarrheal infection caused by ingestion of water or food contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Clinical manifestations range from asymptomatic carriage to profuse, watery diarrhea characterized by a distinctive rice water appearance. The elaboration of toxins leads to rapid fluid and electrolyte depletion, precipitating severe dehydration and potential circulatory collapse if untreated.
pages.caption: Typical cholera diarrhea that looks like "rice water"

pages.text: Transmission dynamics are heavily influenced by environmental and socioeconomic factors, with inadequate sanitation and compromised water infrastructure serving as primary drivers. The pathogen frequently persists in aquatic reservoirs, associating with zooplankton and shellfish. Furthermore, climate change has been implicated in the increasing frequency and intensity of modern global outbreaks.

pages.text: Host susceptibility is modulated by various physiological parameters, including gastric acidity levels, blood type O predisposition, and baseline immune status. Upon ingestion, surviving bacteria traverse the acidic gastric environment, downregulating metabolic processes before penetrating the intestinal mucus layer to colonize the epithelial walls of the small intestine.
